title: Normal Distributions: Finding Values

blocks.title: Finding Z-Scores Given an Area
teacherCues: Ask: 'If 10% of the data lies above a certain value, how do we find that value?'
Write on board: given area → find z-score using table (reverse lookup).

discoveryHook.scenario: A university wants to know the lowest test score for the top 10% of applicants. Or a medical researcher needs the cutoff for the middle 90% of patients by age. When you know the probability and need the value, you work backward through the normal table to find the z-score first!

explanation: In Section 5.2, you found probabilities from x-values. Now you will find x-values from probabilities.
Step 1: Find the z-score that corresponds to the given cumulative area using the Standard Normal Table.
To find a z-score from an area, locate the area inside the table, then read the row and column to determine the z-score.
If the area is not in the table, use the closest entry. If halfway between two entries, use the z-score halfway between the corresponding z-scores.
For right-tail areas, subtract from 1 to get the cumulative area to the left.

formulaCard.title: Z-Score from Area
notes: For right-tail, first convert: cumulative = $1 - $ right area.

examples.title: A – Cumulative Area to Z-Score
examples.prompt: Find the z-score that corresponds to a cumulative area of 0.3632.
steps: Locate 0.3632 in the body of the Standard Normal Table.
The row value is -0.3 and the column value is 0.05.

examples.title: B – Right-Tail Area to Z-Score
examples.prompt: Find the z-score that has 10.75% of the distribution's area to its right.
examples.peerPrompt: Explain to a partner: Why must you subtract 0.1075 from 1 before looking in the table?
steps: Locate 0.8925 in table: row 1.2, column 0.04, so $z = 1.24$.

examples.title: C – Finding Percentile Z-Score
examples.prompt: Find the z-score for the 90th percentile, $P_{90}$.

confusionCorner.title: Left vs. Right Area
confusionCorner.body: The table always works with cumulative area to the left. If given a right-tail area, always subtract from 1 before looking up the z-score.

questions.prompt: To find a z-score from a right-tail area, first subtract the area from ___ to get the cumulative area.
questions.feedbackIfWrong: Subtract from 1 to get the left-tail cumulative area.

questions.prompt: What z-score corresponds to a cumulative area of 0.5?
hints: Half the area is on each side.

questions.prompt: Find the z-score for the 5th percentile, $P_5$.

blocks.title: Transforming a Z-Score to an X-Value
teacherCues: Start with $z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}$. Solve for x: $x = \mu + z\sigma$.

discoveryHook.scenario: You've found the z-score, but what does it mean in the original units? A z-score of 1.96 for cat weights means something very different for dog weights. Converting back to the original x-value brings the answer to life!

explanation: Once you have a z-score, you can convert it back to an x-value using the formula $$ x = \mu + z\sigma $$
This formula is obtained by solving $ z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma} $ for $x$.
$\mu$ is the mean, $\sigma$ is the standard deviation, and $z$ is the z-score.
Positive z-scores give x-values above the mean; negative z-scores give x-values below the mean.
The x-value is in the original units of the data.

examples.title: A – Convert Z to X
examples.prompt: Cat weights are normally distributed with $\mu = 9$ pounds and $\sigma = 2$ pounds. Find the weight for $z = 1.96$.
steps: So the weight is 12.92 pounds, above the mean.

examples.title: B – Negative Z-Score
examples.prompt: For the same cats, find the weight for $z = -0.44$.
examples.peerPrompt: Explain to a partner: Why does a negative z-score give a weight below the mean?
steps: The weight is 8.12 pounds, below the mean.

examples.title: C – Dog Weights
examples.prompt: Dog weights have $\mu = 52$ pounds, $\sigma = 15$ pounds. Find the weight for $z = 3.10$.

confusionCorner.title: Don't Forget the Units
confusionCorner.body: The x-value is in the original units (pounds, inches, etc.), not in z-scores. Always include units in your interpretation.

questions.prompt: The formula to convert a z-score to an x-value is $x = \mu + z \cdot $ ___.

hints: Multiply z by sigma, then add mean.

blocks.title: Finding a Specific Data Value for a Given Probability
teacherCues: Combine the two steps: area → z-score → x-value.
Use the top 10% example: find z for area 0.9, then x = μ + zσ.

discoveryHook.scenario: An agency will only hire applicants in the top 10% of exam scores. What is the lowest score you can earn and still be hired? You must work backward: 10% above means 90% below, find that z-score, then convert to a score. That's the full process!

explanation: To find a specific data value $x$ for a given probability:
Step 1: Determine the cumulative area from the given probability (e.g., top 10% means cumulative area = 0.90).
Step 2: Find the z-score that corresponds to that cumulative area using the table.
Step 3: Convert the z-score to an x-value using $ x = \mu + z\sigma $.
This process answers questions like 'What value separates the top 10% from the rest?'

visuals.title: Steps for Finding Data Value from Probability

formulaCard.title: Probability to X-Value
notes: Top p% means cumulative area = $1 - p/100$.

examples.title: A – Top 10% Score
examples.prompt: Scores for a test are normally distributed with $\mu = 50$ and $\sigma = 10$. An agency hires applicants in the top 10%. What is the lowest score you can earn and still be hired?

examples.title: B – Bottom 1% Cholesterol
examples.prompt: Women ages 20-34 have mean cholesterol 188 mg/dL with $\sigma = 41.3$. Find the highest cholesterol level in the bottom 1%.
examples.peerPrompt: Explain to a partner: Why does 'bottom 1%' correspond to a cumulative area of 0.01?
steps: The highest level in bottom 1% is about 92 mg/dL.

examples.title: C – Longest Braking Distance in Bottom 1%
examples.prompt: Braking distances of Nissan Altimas are normally distributed with $\mu = 129$ feet, $\sigma = 5.18$ feet. What is the longest braking distance in the bottom 1%?
steps: The longest distance in bottom 1% is about 117 feet.

confusionCorner.title: Top vs. Bottom
confusionCorner.body: For 'top p%', the cumulative area is $1 - p/100$. For 'bottom p%', the cumulative area is $p/100$. Getting this backward reverses the answer.

questions.prompt: To find the value separating the top 10%, the cumulative area to use is ___.
For bottom 5%, what cumulative area do you use?

blocks.title: Percentiles and Cutoff Values
teacherCues: Ask: 'What does the 95th percentile mean in terms of area below?'
Demonstrate finding height for 95th percentile and first quartile.

discoveryHook.scenario: Percentiles are everywhere—test scores, baby growth charts, and medical measurements. The 95th percentile for height means 95% of people are shorter. Normal distributions let you find the actual measurement that corresponds to any percentile!

explanation: A [[kw:percentile]] $P_k$ is the value below which $k$% of the data falls.
To find the value for a given percentile, convert the percentile to a cumulative area: $P_k$ means area = $k/100$.
Find the z-score for that cumulative area using the table.
Convert the z-score to an x-value: $ x = \mu + z\sigma $.
Common percentiles: quartiles (25th, 50th, 75th), 90th, 95th, 99th.

formulaCard.title: Percentile to X-Value
notes: Area is always to the left.

examples.title: A – 95th Percentile Height
examples.prompt: Women's heights have $\mu = 64.3$ inches, $\sigma = 2.6$ inches. What height represents the 95th percentile?
steps: The 95th percentile height is about 68.6 inches.

examples.title: B – First Quartile
examples.prompt: Using the same data, find the first quartile (25th percentile).
examples.peerPrompt: Explain to a partner: Why does the first quartile have a negative z-score?

examples.title: C – Middle 50%
examples.prompt: Sleeping times have $\mu = 6.1$ hours, $\sigma = 1.0$ hour. Between what two values does the middle 50% lie?

confusionCorner.title: Middle vs. Tail Areas
confusionCorner.body: For the middle 50%, you need two z-scores: one for the 25th percentile and one for the 75th percentile. The area in each tail is 25%.

questions.prompt: The 25th percentile is also known as the first ___.
hints: It divides data into four parts.

questions.prompt: For the 75th percentile, what cumulative area do you use?
What z-score corresponds to the median (50th percentile)?

blocks.title: Blueprint Aid – Solving Normal Distribution Value Problems
teacherCues: Display Understand → Solve → Conclude. Walk through a full value-finding problem: top 10%, find cutoff.
Emphasize: Understand identifies percentile/area; Solve finds z then x; Conclude interprets in context.

discoveryHook.scenario: Finding values from probabilities involves two reverse steps: area to z-score, then z-score to x-value. The blueprint keeps you organized so you don't confuse left and right tails or skip a step!

explanation: [[imp:Understand]] – Read the problem. Is it asking for a value that separates the top or bottom percentage? Determine the cumulative area. Identify $\mu$ and $\sigma$.
[[imp:Solve]] – Step 1: Find the z-score for the cumulative area using the table or invNorm. Step 2: Convert to x-value using $x = \mu + z\sigma$.
[[imp:Conclude]] – State the value in context. Check if it is unusual (|z| > 2). Interpret the result.

formulaCard.title: Reverse Normal Formula
notes: Use invNorm on TI-83/84 for z-score.

examples.title: A – Full Blueprint: Top 10%
examples.prompt: Use blueprint: Test scores have $\mu = 50$, $\sigma = 10$. Find the lowest score for the top 10%.
steps: Conclude: Lowest score for top 10% is about 63.

examples.title: B – Full Blueprint: Bottom 5%
examples.prompt: Use blueprint: Waiting times have $\mu = 204$ days, $\sigma = 25.7$ days. Find the 5th percentile.
examples.peerPrompt: Explain to a partner: Why does the 5th percentile use a negative z-score?
steps: Conclude: The 5th percentile waiting time is about 162 days.

examples.title: C – Decide and Compute
examples.prompt: Use blueprint: Apple consumption has $\mu = 16.2$ pounds, $\sigma = 4$ pounds. Find the smallest consumption in the top 25%.
steps: Conclude: The smallest top 25% consumption is about 18.9 pounds.

confusionCorner.title: Two-Step Process
confusionCorner.body: Always remember there are two steps: area → z-score, then z-score → x-value. Skipping either step leads to incorrect answers.

questions.prompt: In the Understand phase, what must you determine from 'top 10%'?
hints: It is the area to the left.

questions.prompt: In the Solve phase, first find the ___ from the area, then convert to x using $x = \mu + z\sigma$.
If $\mu = 100$, $\sigma = 15$, and the z-score for the 90th percentile is 1.28, what is the 90th percentile value? Round to one decimal place.

presenterNotes: Start with the reverse table lookup. Many students find this harder than forward lookup, so practice several examples.
Emphasize the two-step process: area → z-score, then z-score → x-value. Use sketches to clarify left vs. right tails.
Connect to percentiles and quartiles. Students should recognize common z-scores for 5th, 25th, 75th, and 95th percentiles.
Use technology (invNorm) to check table-based answers.
The blueprint is especially useful here because of the multi-step nature of these problems.
